cause_plain: Calling url_for with a URL value named "self" crashes with a confusing TypeError. Python reads that keyword as the method's own "self" argument, so the call fails before any URL is built.
cause_technical: Flask.url_for in src/flask/app.py (line 953) declares `self` as a normal positional-or-keyword parameter. `helpers.url_for` forwards `**values` containing `self=1`, which collides with the bound `self`. Making `self` positional-only (`self, /, endpoint`) lets `self` be passed through `**values` as a URL or query value.
real_cause: Flask.url_for() declared self as an ordinary parameter, so a URL value named 'self' passed via **values collided with it; the fix makes self positional-only.

cause_plain: The app crashes at startup. One route is declared with status 204 (No Content), and FastAPI took the function's return type hint as a response body model. A 204 response can't have a body, so FastAPI refused to load the app.
cause_technical: In fastapi/routing.py APIRoute.__init__ (line ~472-477), when response_model is not given, it is inferred from the endpoint's return annotation. This happens without checking the status code. For a 204 route with an annotation such as `-> dict`, response_model becomes truthy. The assert at line 514 then fails. The fix is to skip inferring a response model when the status code doesn't allow a body.
real_cause: get_typed_annotation() turned the string annotation 'None' (from postponed annotations) into NoneType rather than None, so the route was treated as having a response body and the 204 assertion failed.

cause_plain: When a POST got a redirect (such as 301, 302 or 303), the client turned it into a GET with no body. It still sent the old Content-Length header from the POST. The request then promised 5 bytes and sent none, so it failed.
cause_technical: In httpx/middleware.py, build_redirect_request (line 91) copies the original request headers through redirect_headers. When the method changes to GET, redirect_content (line 157) returns b
real_cause: RedirectMiddleware.redirect_headers() kept Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding when a redirect switched the method to GET and dropped the body, so h11 saw too little data for the declared length.

cause_plain: Black crashed while formatting a file. It checked how deeply a piece of code is nested inside brackets, but some pieces never had that value recorded. This happens with a closing bracket that has no matching opening bracket on the same line, or with a comment.
cause_technical: BracketTracker.mark in src/black/brackets.py returns early at lines 89-97 for COMMENT leaves and for unmatched closing brackets at depth 0. It returns before `leaf.bracket_depth = self.depth` (line 113), so those leaves have no `bracket_depth`. is_line_short_enough in src/black/lines.py (about line 1404) reads `leaf.bracket_depth` on every leaf of a line that contains a multiline string. That raises AttributeError for any leaf that was skipped. I could not confirm which of the two cases triggered this event. The fix is to set `bracket_depth` before each early return. The exact line numbers in lines.py differ slightly from the traceback (1279 vs about 1404).
real_cause: blib2to3 Leaf declared bracket_depth only as an annotation and neither __init__ nor clone() set it, so leaves created outside the bracket tracker lacked the attribute that is_line_short_enough() reads.

cause_plain: Defining an attrs class failed with a SyntaxError when the class has an `__attrs_pre_init__` that takes arguments and has at least one keyword-only field with a default value. attrs builds the class's `__init__` as source code, and that code was invalid.
cause_technical: In `_attrs_to_init_script` (src/attr/_make.py, around lines 2204-2219), `kw_only_args` and `args` hold full parameter declarations such as `y=NOTHING`. The pre-init call builds its arguments from those strings. `f"{kw_arg}={kw_arg}"` produces `y=NOTHING=y=NOTHING`, which is a SyntaxError when `compile` runs. Positional entries like `x=NOTHING` are also copied into the call, so a default sentinel would be passed instead of the value. The call should use bare parameter names only. I did not open `attrs_pre_init.py`, so this rests on the stack trace and the generator code.
real_cause: _attrs_to_init_script() built the __attrs_pre_init__ call from kw_only argument strings that still included '=default', generating invalid code like a=attr_dict['a'].default=a=....
